items.stem: The dependency ratio is calculated as
options: the number unemployed divided by the labour force
the population divided by the land area
the number of children per family
the number of people aged under 15 and over 64 divided by the number aged 15 to 64, × 100
items.answer: the number of people aged under 15 and over 64 divided by the number aged 15 to 64, × 100
items.markingKey: Dependants per 100 people of working age.

items.stem: Explain two economic problems caused by a high dependency ratio of young people.
items.answer: High spending needed on education and health; fewer workers to support dependants; low saving; pressure on jobs when they enter the labour force.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each identified, 1 mark each explained [4]

items.stem: Explain why birth rates tend to fall as countries develop.
items.answer: Lower infant mortality, more education and employment for women, access to contraception, children cost more and are needed less for farm work or old-age support, urbanisation.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each reason [2]

items.stem: In Pelora, 35% of the population is aged under 15, 22% is over 64 and the rest are aged 15–64. Calculate the dependency ratio.

Valdoria: 28% of the population aged under 15, 8% over 64. Birth rate 24 per 1,000; death rate 12 per 1,000; net migration -1 per 1,000. Calculate the dependency ratio, the natural rate of increase and the population growth rate (%), and the approximate doubling time. Explain one economic implication.
items.answer: Dependency ratio = 56.2; natural increase = 12 per 1,000 (1.2%); growth = 1.1%; doubling time ≈ 64 years. A young population needs heavy spending on schools and jobs.
items.markingKey: Dependency ratio [1]; natural increase [1]; growth incl. migration [1]; rule of 70 [1]; implication [1].

items.stem: Extract: In Valdoria, 35% of the population is under 15 and 5% over 64. 60% of workers are in agriculture, many in the informal sector, and the urban population is growing by 5% a year. (a) Calculate the dependency ratio. (b) Explain why rapid urbanisation may increase the informal economy.
items.answer: (a) 66.7 (b) Migrants exceed formal job creation; informal work and housing absorb them.

items.stem: The natural rate of population increase is
options: the birth rate minus the death rate
items.answer: the birth rate minus the death rate
items.markingKey: Excludes migration; usually per 1,000.

items.stem: The birth rate in Calvania has fallen sharply over 20 years. Explain how this could create a demographic dividend.
items.answer: As fewer children are born, the working-age share rises and the dependency ratio falls, so more people produce and save relative to dependants, raising income per head if jobs are available.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: lower dependency; 1 mark: more workers/saving → growth [2]

Calculate the dependency ratio, the natural rate of increase and the population growth rate (%), and the approximate doubling time. Explain one economic implication.
items.answer: Dependency ratio = 56.2; natural increase = 12 per 1,000 (1.2%); growth = 1.4%; doubling time ≈ 50 years. A young population needs heavy spending on schools and jobs.

items.stem: (a) Explain the meaning and significance of the dependency ratio. (b) Discuss the extent to which rapid population growth is the main obstacle to economic development.
items.answer: (a) Explanation of the theory (with a described diagram where relevant), drawing on: High dependency, pressure on resources, low saving. (b) Case for the view: High dependency, pressure on resources, low saving. Case against / evaluation: Demographic dividend; larger labour force and market; other obstacles (institutions, infrastructure, debt). Conclusion: a judgement on the conditions under which the view holds.
items.markingKey: (a) Knowledge and understanding of the theory, clear analytical chain; diagram described accurately with labelled axes and curves. (b) Analysis of arguments for and against; evaluation reaches a justified conclusion that weighs the conditions under which the claim holds. Top level needs a judgement, not just a summary.

items.stem: In most low-income countries, the largest share of employment is in the
items.answer: primary sector
items.markingKey: Agriculture, fishing, mining.

items.stem: Explain why employment shifts from the primary sector as an economy develops.
items.answer: Agricultural productivity rises so fewer workers are needed; income elasticity of demand for food is low while that for manufactures and services is high; urban jobs pay more.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: productivity; 1 mark: income elasticities; 1 mark: wage differences [3]

items.stem: Explain one problem for a country with a large share of employment in agriculture.
items.answer: Low productivity and incomes; vulnerability to weather and commodity prices; underemployment and seasonal unemployment.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: problem; 1 mark: explanation [2]

items.stem: In Fendaria, 20 million people are employed: 62% in the primary sector and 20% in the secondary sector. Calculate the number employed in the tertiary sector.
items.answer: 3.6 million
items.markingKey: Tertiary = 18% × 20 = 3.6 million.

items.stem: In Korvia, 45% of the 20 million workers are in the primary sector, which produces 25% of GDP. 10% work in industry and the rest in services. Calculate the number of workers in each sector and the productivity of primary-sector workers relative to the rest of the economy. Explain what this suggests about the country’s level of development.
items.answer: Primary 9m, secondary 2m, tertiary 9m. Relative productivity = (25/45) ÷ (75/55) = 0.41. Low productivity in a large primary sector is typical of a low-income economy; moving labour out of agriculture would raise output.
items.markingKey: Workers in each sector [2]; relative productivity ratio [2]; interpretation [1].

options: from the primary to the secondary and then the tertiary sector

items.stem: Explain why Lunaria’s share of employment in services has risen as incomes have grown.
items.answer: Demand for services (health, finance, leisure) is income elastic, so it rises faster than income; productivity gains in agriculture and manufacturing release labour.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: YED; 1 mark: productivity releases labour [2]

items.answer: 4 million

items.stem: In Valdoria, 62% of the 25 million workers are in the primary sector, which produces 8% of GDP. 20% work in industry and the rest in services. Calculate the number of workers in each sector and the productivity of primary-sector workers relative to the rest of the economy. Explain what this suggests about the country’s level of development.
items.answer: Primary 15.5m, secondary 5m, tertiary 4.5m. Relative productivity = (8/62) ÷ (92/38) = 0.05. Low productivity in a large primary sector is typical of a low-income economy; moving labour out of agriculture would raise output.

items.stem: The informal economy consists of
options: economic activity that is not registered, taxed or regulated by the state
activity of large registered firms only
items.answer: economic activity that is not registered, taxed or regulated by the state
items.markingKey: E.g. street vendors, casual labour.

items.stem: Explain two disadvantages of a large informal economy.
items.answer: Low tax revenue for public services; workers lack legal protection, social insurance and access to credit; low productivity; GDP data unreliable.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each identified, 1 mark each explained [4]

items.stem: Explain why income inequality is often high in countries at an early stage of development.
items.answer: Ownership of land and capital is concentrated; small modern sector with high wages alongside large low-productivity sector; limited taxes and transfers (Kuznets curve).
items.markingKey: 1 mark: dual economy/ownership; 1 mark: weak redistribution [2]

items.stem: Rovania has a population of 30 million, of whom 30% live in urban areas. Calculate the urban population.

items.stem: Over 15 years, Quentara’s population grew from 30 million to 36 million and the urban share from 30% to 45%. The informal economy is estimated at 30% of official GDP of $100 billion. items.answer: Urban: 9m → 16.2m (80%). Informal economy ≈ $30 billion. Consequence: pressure on housing, transport and services; growth of slums and informal jobs; lower tax base.
